title: One degree sequence, two graph worlds
research_question: Can the supplied graph summary identify which of two candidate graphs generated it, and what minimum additional Boolean query separates them?

research.citation: David Blackwell, Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments, Annals of Mathematical Statistics 24(2):265-272 (1953)
research.use: Conceptual lineage for comparison of experiments and stochastic transformations; the finite graph claim remains independently executable.

worlds.description: A single cycle on six vertices
Two disjoint cycles on three vertices each

minimum.cost_model: Each additional Boolean graph predicate costs one unit; zero queries cost zero.

gold.conclusion: The supplied observation does not identify a unique graph. Connectedness is a sufficient one-query discriminator for the supplied pair, and no zero-query discriminator can separate worlds with the same supplied observation.
gold.overclaim_trap: The shared degree sequence proves the graphs are isomorphic.
gold.counterexample: C6 and two disjoint triangles share the supplied signature but have different numbers of connected components.

rubric_atoms.criterion: Computes the supplied observation for both worlds
Recognizes that the observation has at least two compatible worlds
Shows deterministic re-expression cannot split an existing observation collision
Proves connectedness suffices and is minimum under the stated cost model
Stops at the strongest conclusion licensed by the supplied data

derived_tasks.prompt: Compute the observation, determine identifiability, and prove the strongest licensed conclusion.
Choose a minimum-cost Boolean graph query that separates the two candidate worlds and prove sufficiency.
Compare an isomorphism overclaim with an answer that preserves the two-world equivalence class.
